opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting puzzles in robotics right now. If you look at the last few years, locomotion has made enormous progress. Quadrupeds can run, climb stairs, hike up mountains, and now humanoids can walk, do backflips, even dance. But when you ask a robot to do something that a three-year-old child can do with its hands, like tying a shoelace or picking up a coin from a table, it's still very hard.

I see a few reasons for this gap.

The first is about the nature of the problem. Locomotion, at its core, is about controlling your own body. The robot interacts with the environment mainly through its feet and the ground, and the ground is relatively simple. It's mostly rigid, and the contact patterns are fairly regular. So you can model the physics reasonably well, and that's why simulation-to-real transfer works so well for locomotion. We can train a policy in simulation with reinforcement learning, with millions of trials, and deploy it on the real robot almost zero-shot.

Manipulation is very different. The point of manipulation is to change the world, not just to move yourself. You interact with an enormous variety of objects: rigid, soft, deformable, articulated, liquids, cloth. Each has different shapes, materials, friction, weight. The contacts are rich and complex. Many fingers touching an object at the same time, sliding, rolling. That's very hard to simulate accurately, so the sim-to-real gap is much bigger. The recipe that worked so well for locomotion doesn't transfer as easily.

The second reason is perception and generalization. For walking, you mostly need to know your own body state and roughly what the terrain looks like. For manipulation, you need to understand what the object is, where to grasp it, what the task means, and often what the human wants. That requires semantic understanding of the world, which is a very different kind of intelligence.

The third reason is hardware. Legs are relatively mature now. Motors are strong enough, and the designs have converged. Hands are still far from human-level. The human hand has over twenty degrees of freedom, dense tactile sensing all over the skin, and it's very robust. Robot hands are either simple and robust, like grippers, or dexterous and fragile and expensive. And we still lack good tactile sensing at scale.

And finally, data. For locomotion, simulation gives us almost unlimited data. For manipulation, since simulation is less reliable, people rely more on real-world data, teleoperation, human videos. That data is expensive and slow to collect, and there's no internet-scale dataset of robot actions the way there is for text or images.

So my view is that locomotion is close to being a "solved" problem in the sense that we have a recipe that works. Manipulation is where the real frontier is. And I think progress there will come from combining several things: large foundation models that bring semantic understanding and common sense, better simulation, better hardware especially hands and touch, and smarter ways to collect and use data. That combination is what many of us are working toward, and I'm quite optimistic we'll see big leaps in the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response calls locomotion close to solved and describes reinforcement learning policies trained in simulation as the recipe behind its progress.

r002.rationale: It says dexterous manipulation remains very hard and is the real frontier, indicating that a good solution has yet to be found.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, because from the outside it looks like a paradox. Legged robots can now run, climb stairs, recover from being pushed, do backflips. And yet if you ask the same robot to pick up a pen and put the cap back on, it struggles. So why is the "lower body" so far ahead of the "upper body"?

I think there are a few reasons, and they're related.

The first is the dimensionality and nature of contact. Locomotion is actually a fairly structured contact problem. A quadruped has four feet, the feet touch the ground, the ground is mostly flat or at least large and rigid, and contact events happen in a rhythm. You can describe much of walking with a gait pattern. Manipulation is the opposite. A dexterous hand has twenty or more degrees of freedom, and the contact can happen anywhere on the fingertip, on the palm, on the side of a finger. The object is small, it can be deformable, it can slip, it can rotate in your hand. Every grasp is almost a new contact configuration. So the space of things that can happen is just enormously larger, and contact is much harder to model and to simulate.

The second reason is simulation and sim-to-real. A big part of why locomotion took off in the last several years is that we figured out how to train policies in simulation with reinforcement learning, randomize the physics, and transfer them to real robots. That works well for legs because the simulation is good enough. Foot-ground contact with a rigid body simulator is reasonably faithful. For hands, the simulators are much less accurate. Friction, soft fingertips, deformable objects, tiny geometric details that decide whether an object slips or not — these are exactly the things physics engines get wrong. So the reality gap is wider, and the trick that worked for locomotion doesn't transfer directly.

The third reason is hardware. Legs are, mechanically, a relatively mature design problem. A few motors, big and strong, relatively easy to make robust. A human-like hand is a nightmare to build. You want many actuators in a very small volume, you want tactile sensing across the whole surface, you want compliance, and you want it to survive being banged against a table thousands of times. Most dexterous hands today are either expensive and fragile or cheap and very limited. Honestly, I think we underestimate how much of the gap is not an algorithm problem but a hardware problem. The sensing especially — humans rely heavily on touch for manipulation, and most robot hands are nearly blind in that sense.

And the fourth reason is the task definition. Locomotion has a clear, almost universal objective: get from here to there without falling. You can write that as a reward. Manipulation is really thousands of different tasks — folding cloth, opening a jar, inserting a connector, using tools — and each one has different success criteria. So it's harder to get a single scalable learning recipe. This is why you now see people turning to large-scale data collection, teleoperation, and foundation models, because the hope is that data can substitute for the structure we don't have.

So my overall view is that the gap is not surprising. Locomotion was the "easier" problem in the sense that the right ingredients — decent simulation, robust hardware, a simple objective, RL — all lined up around the same time. For manipulation, those ingredients are not yet aligned. But I'm actually optimistic. The progress in locomotion taught us a methodology, and now the community is working hard on exactly the missing pieces: better simulation of contact, better and more affordable hands with tactile sensing, and large-scale data. When those catch up, I think we'll see manipulation have its own "moment," similar to what legged robots went through a few years ago.

r001.rationale: The response describes substantial locomotion progress and says reinforcement learning helped it take off, but it does not judge that reinforcement learning has essentially solved locomotion.

r002.rationale: The response says manipulation remains difficult, its key ingredients are not yet aligned, and the field is still working on missing pieces, communicating that a good general solution has not yet been found.

astra-6.text:
I think the difference comes down to the structure of the problems. Locomotion is difficult, but the task is relatively consistent: keep your balance and move across the ground. We can train a policy across many variations of terrain, and the basic objective stays the same.

Manipulation is much more open-ended. Picking up a cup, folding a shirt, and connecting a cable involve very different objects, contact patterns, and goals. A hand also has many degrees of freedom, and small errors in contact can determine whether a task succeeds or fails. You need to understand not just where an object is, but how it will respond when you touch it.

Simulation is another important difference. We can simulate many aspects of locomotion well enough for learning to transfer to a real robot. With manipulation, friction, deformation, and fine contact are often harder to model accurately. And collecting that experience on real hardware is slow.

So I wouldn’t say locomotion is solved, but it has a more mature training pipeline. For manipulation, we still need better ways to combine perception, touch, and large amounts of diverse experience. That makes progress less uniform, even when individual demonstrations look very impressive.

r001.rationale: The response says locomotion is not solved, while describing its training pipeline as more mature. It does not judge that reinforcement learning has essentially solved locomotion.

r002.rationale: It says manipulation still needs better methods for combining perception, touch, and diverse experience, communicating that a good solution has yet to be found.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difference comes partly from the structure of the problems. Locomotion is difficult, but the objective is relatively clear: keep your balance and move at a desired velocity. And walking is repetitive, so a policy can reuse similar patterns over and over.

Manipulation has much more variety. You might pick up a cup, fold a shirt, or insert a connector. Each task involves different objects, different contacts, and different definitions of success. Even a small change in friction or the position of a fingertip can change the outcome. You also need to understand what the object is and what you want to do with it.

Simulation is another factor. For locomotion, we can often build simulations that are useful enough to train a policy and transfer it to a real robot. With hands, accurately simulating all those contacts—especially with soft or deformable objects—is much harder. Tactile sensing and reliable hand hardware are also challenging.

So I wouldn’t say manipulation is simply a few years behind locomotion on the same path. It has additional problems to solve. The progress in locomotion gives us useful tools, but dexterous manipulation will also need better sensing, better hardware, and much broader training experience.

r001.rationale: The response calls locomotion difficult and describes useful training and transfer, but never says reinforcement learning has essentially solved it.

r002.rationale: The response says manipulation has additional problems to solve and will need better sensing, hardware, and broader training experience, conveying that a good solution has not yet been found.
